newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to stay out of NATO military wing for now.
newsitem.headline: France to stay out of NATO military wing for now.

text.p: Next week's NATO summit in Madrid was supposed to seal an historic reconciliation between France and the Atlantic alliance, with Paris returning to the integrated military command in exchange for a bigger role for Europe.
It's not going to happen. At least not for now.
Instead, to the dismay of its European allies, the two-day meeting of allied leaders may highlight acrimony between France and the United States.

Despite some U.S. concessions towards the development of a European defence identity, Paris says Washington is unwilling to share real power with the Europeans and wants to dictate the future shape of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation single-handedly.
"There's going to be some blunt speaking in Madrid," a French official forecast.

A statement approved by both conservative President Jacques Chirac and Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said on Wednesday that France considered that the conditions for its return to NATO's military wing had not been met.

It also contradicted Washington by saying that five former communist east European countries qualified to join an enlarged NATO, and not just the three -- the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland -- that the United States wants to admit.
French officials were irked by a New York Times report on Thursday saying Paris had effectively accepted Washington's position and would not block the entry of those three states.
Aides said Chirac had never threatened to block their entry and would still press for Romania and Slovenia to join.
Asked if there was a consensus with Washington on three entrants, Foreign Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux said on Thursday: "There is no consensus on three, four or five."

Paris had demanded that the United States hand over NATO's southern command, which controls the Mediterranean, to the Europeans as the price for rejoining the integrated military structure it quit in 1966 under then president Charles de Gaulle.

Chirac, who sees himself as De Gaulle's political heir, launched a rapprochement with NATO after his election in 1995 after concluding that France would never persuade its European partners to build a joint defence outside the alliance.
But he appeared to overplay his hand by demanding a higher price than U.S. President Bill Clinton could or would pay.
The Socialists, then in opposition, accused Chirac of botching the negotiations by making concessions to the Americans without winning anything substantial in exchange.

While Paris failed to wring greater power-sharing in talks with Washington, it also failed to persuade the European Union at last month's Amsterdam summit to take a significant step towards a common European defence policy despite German backing.
"As a result, the European Union in Madrid will have not one face but several faces, which is itself a step backwards," said former European Commission president Jacques Delors.

France's closest friends, notably in Germany, and some of its own leading strategists are urging Paris not to return to the latent anti-Americanism which lurks just below the surface of the French political establishment.

"You cannot build European unity against the United States. The way the French see America doesn't correspond to the way the other Europeans see it," said Dominique Moisi of the French Institute for International Relations.

"I fear that since the last French election, there is a risk of a competitive escalation on the subject of the United States between Mr Chirac and Mr Jospin," Moisi said. "Neither wants to appear softer than the other on the United States."
In the long term, France would only be isolating itself if it did not return to NATO's military wing because "we need the Americans more than they need us," he argued.
Officials said Chirac hoped that negotiations with the United States would resume and a compromise would eventually be found enabling a full French role in NATO's military structure.

They noted Washington had made some progress by accepting that a European deputy Supreme Allied Commander in Europe would command operations, using NATO assets and infrastructure, in which the Americans chose not to participate.
A European chain of command would be indentified within the NATO structure to enable so-called Combined Joint Task Forces to carry out such missions.
